learn.hook: Add 4,786 and 3,459 by counting dots? You'd still be counting at dinner time! Column addition finishes in seconds.
points: Counting dots works for tiny numbers but becomes impossibly slow as numbers grow; column addition stays fast because the work depends on the number of digits, not the size of the number.
Column addition: line the numbers up by place value, add the units first, write the units digit of the sum and carry any ten to the next column, move left, and write the final carry at the end.
It works because of place value: 10 units make 1 ten, 10 tens make 1 hundred, and so on. Carrying is regrouping.
Adding two 4-digit numbers needs just 4 column steps, while counting dots would need thousands of counts.
learn.reallife: Shopkeepers adding a bill in a notebook use the same column method you learnt in primary school.

quiz.q: Why is column addition faster than counting dots for big numbers?
options: Its steps depend on the number of digits, not the size of the number
quiz.explain: A 6-digit sum takes about 6 column steps, while counting would take hundreds of thousands of counts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both take the same time

quiz.explain: Units 12 (carry 1), tens 6 + 7 + 1 = 14 (carry 1), hundreds 8 + 5 + 1 = 14 (carry 1), thousands 5 + 2 + 1 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add a carry

quiz.q: In 468 + 375, what is written in the tens place of the answer?
quiz.explain: Units: 8 + 5 = 13, carry 1. Tens: 6 + 7 + 1 = 14, write 4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the carry from the units

quiz.q: When adding by columns, which column do you start with?
options: The column with the biggest digits
quiz.explain: Carries move leftwards, so you must start from the right.
quiz.mistake: Starts from the left and has to go back

quiz.q: What does 'carrying 1' into the tens column really mean?
quiz.explain: Place value: ten units equal one ten.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a carry is a rule with no meaning

quiz.q: About how many basic steps would counting on from 3,000 by ones take to add 3,000 + 2,000?
quiz.explain: You would count 2,000 more ones; column addition needs only 4 column steps.
quiz.mistake: Thinks counting is as fast as columns

quiz.q: What is the final carry written when adding 875 + 649?
quiz.explain: 5 + 9 = 14 (carry 1); 7 + 4 + 1 = 12 (carry 1); 8 + 6 + 1 = 15 (write 5, carry 1). The sum is 1524.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to write the last carry

quiz.q: Riya adds 4999 + 2 by columns. How many carries does she make?
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first carry

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How does column addition work, and why do we carry?"
teach.praise: Super! Start from the units, and carry because 10 of one place make 1 of the next!
teach.nudge: Which column do you start with? What does the carry stand for?

learn.hook: A recipe for chai, the steps for long division and the instructions inside your phone's map app have something in common: they are all algorithms!
points: An algorithm is a finite list of clear, step-by-step instructions that solves a problem or completes a task.
A good algorithm has an input (what you start with), an output (the result), and steps that are precise, so anyone following them gets the same result.
It must stop after a finite number of steps.
The order of steps matters: 'add 3, then double' is not the same as 'double, then add 3'.
Algorithms can repeat steps (loops) and make choices (if this, then do that).

example.q: Algorithm: start with a number. If it is even, halve it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Stop when you reach 1. Start with 6. How many steps until you reach 1?

learn.reallife: Railway ticket booking, ATM cash withdrawal and traffic signals all run on algorithms written by programmers.

games.title: Algorithm for making chai
items: Boil a cup of water in a pan
Add tea leaves and let it boil for a minute
Add milk and sugar and boil again
Strain the chai into a cup

games.title: Clear step or vague step?
items: Do something nice with the number
Keep going until it feels right

quiz.q: Which is the best description of an algorithm?
options: A finite list of clear steps that solves a problem
Any computer program, even one that never stops
A list of answers to memorise
quiz.explain: An algorithm must be step-by-step, precise and finite.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only computer code can be an algorithm

quiz.q: Which instruction would be a poor step in an algorithm?
options: Stop when the total is above 100
quiz.explain: 'A little' and 'maybe' are vague; two people could follow this step differently.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that a step must be precise

quiz.q: Start with 5. Repeat 3 times: double the number and then add 1. What is the result?
quiz.mistake: Stops after two repeats (23) or does one repeat too many (95)

quiz.q: In an algorithm for making chai, what are the inputs?
options: Water, tea leaves, milk and sugar
quiz.explain: Inputs are what the algorithm starts with. The cup of chai is the output.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the input with the output

quiz.q: Use the rule: if even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; stop at 1. Starting from 12, how many steps until you reach 1?
quiz.mistake: Counts the numbers in the chain (10) instead of the steps between them

quiz.q: Why must an algorithm have a finite number of steps?
options: So that it fits on one page
So that it eventually stops and gives an answer
Because computers can only count to 100
quiz.explain: A procedure that never stops can never give an output.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the length limit is about writing space

quiz.q: Algorithm A: add 3, then multiply by 2. Algorithm B: multiply by 2, then add 3. Both start with 5. What is A's result minus B's result?
quiz.explain: A gives (5 + 3) × 2 = 16. B gives 5 × 2 + 3 = 13. 16 − 13 = 3, so order matters.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the order of steps does not change the result

quiz.q: To find the largest number in a list, keep a 'biggest so far' and replace it only when a number is BIGGER. For the list 7, 3, 12, 9, 12, 5, how many times is 'biggest so far' replaced after starting with 7?
quiz.explain: Only the first 12 is bigger than 7. The second 12 is equal, not bigger, so no change.
quiz.mistake: Replaces the value when a number is equal, counting 2

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "My mum's recipe says 'cook till done'. Is that an algorithm?"
teach.praise: An algorithm needs clear, precise steps in the right order that finish with an answer. 'Till done' is too vague for a computer!
teach.nudge: Would two different people understand 'cook till done' in exactly the same way? What makes a step good?

learn.hook: When you add two numbers, can a carry ever be 2? Try your hardest with 9s: it can't!
points: When adding two numbers, a column sum is at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19, so the carry is never more than 1. (With three or more numbers, bigger carries are possible.)
If the numbers have different lengths, treat missing digits as 0: 3456 + 78 is 3456 + 0078.
The written method often skips steps like 'write a 0' or 'no carry'; a full algorithm states them clearly.
For decimals, line up the decimal points (fill missing places with 0), add as usual, and put the point in the same column.
learn.reallife: Adding ₹149.50 and ₹38.75 at a stationery shop is decimal column addition.

games.title: Carry facts
items: Adding two numbers, a carry can be 2.
Adding three numbers, a carry can be 2.
For decimals we line up the last digits.
We line up the decimal points.

quiz.q: What is the largest possible carry when adding two numbers by columns?
quiz.explain: The biggest column total is 9 + 9 + 1 (carry) = 19.
quiz.mistake: Thinks large digits can make a carry of 2

quiz.q: What is the largest possible column total when adding two numbers (including the carry)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the incoming carry

quiz.q: Adding three numbers, what is the largest possible carry from the units column?
quiz.mistake: Applies the two-number rule to three numbers

quiz.explain: Treat 596 as 0596: units 13 (carry 1), tens 2 + 9 + 1 = 12 (carry 1), hundreds 0 + 5 + 1 = 6, thousands 8.
quiz.mistake: Lines up the numbers from the left
Lines up the last digits instead of the decimal points
Ignores the missing thousandths digit

quiz.q: Joseph writes 523 + 41 as 523 + 410. What mistake did he make?
options: He lined up from the left; 41 should be 041
quiz.explain: Units must line up with units: 41 = 041.
quiz.mistake: Thinks digits line up from the left

quiz.q: Kavya buys a pen for ₹45.50 and a notebook for ₹62.75. What is the total?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the carry from the paise

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I add decimals by columns?"
teach.praise: Great! Line up the decimal points, fill gaps with 0, and add with carries!
teach.nudge: What must you line up in decimal addition? What fills an empty place?

learn.hook: Over 2000 years ago Euclid found a way to get the HCF of two huge numbers without listing a single factor. It is still used in every computer today!
points: Division algorithm: for whole numbers a and b > 0, a = b × q + r with 0 ≤ r < b.

Euclid's algorithm for HCF(a, b): divide the larger by the smaller, then replace the pair by (smaller, remainder). Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder (the last divisor) is the HCF.
LCM(a, b) = a × b ÷ HCF(a, b).
To test if n is prime, you only need to try dividing by primes up to √n.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds all primes up to a limit by crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7, ... Binary search finds an item in a sorted list by halving the search area each time.

example.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(252, 105).
steps: The remainder is 0, so the HCF is the last divisor, 21

learn.reallife: Online payments are kept safe by codes that use Euclid's algorithm and prime numbers. Searching a contact on your phone uses ideas like binary search.

quiz.q: Use Euclid's algorithm to find HCF(48, 18).
quiz.mistake: Stops early and gives the first remainder (12)

quiz.q: Find HCF(91, 65) using Euclid's algorithm.
quiz.mistake: Gives a remainder from the middle of the process instead of the last divisor

quiz.q: To check whether 97 is prime, what is the largest prime you need to try dividing by?
quiz.explain: √97 is a little less than 10, so you only need to try 2, 3, 5 and 7. None divides 97, so 97 is prime.
quiz.mistake: Thinks you must try every number up to half of 97

quiz.q: Riya thinks of a number from 1 to 100. Arjun always guesses the middle of the remaining range and is told 'higher' or 'lower'. What is the most guesses he will ever need?
quiz.explain: After each wrong guess at most half of the numbers are left: 100 → 50 → 25 → 12 → 6 → 3 → 1. After 6 guesses only one number can remain, so the 7th guess is sure to be right (2⁷ = 128 ≥ 100).
quiz.mistake: Thinks you might need to try every number one by one

quiz.q: HCF(12, 18) = 6. What is LCM(12, 18)?
quiz.mistake: Gives the product 216 without dividing by the HCF

quiz.q: After using the Sieve of Eratosthenes on the numbers 1 to 100, how many primes are left?
quiz.explain: Crossing out 1 and the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7 (but not those primes themselves) leaves exactly 25 primes up to 100.
quiz.mistake: Thinks half the numbers (all the odd ones) are prime

quiz.q: Use repeated subtraction (the older form of Euclid's method) for HCF(35, 14): keep subtracting the smaller from the larger. What is the HCF?
quiz.explain: (35, 14) → (21, 14) → (7, 14) → (7, 7). When the two numbers are equal, that number, 7, is the HCF.
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first subtraction

quiz.q: Write 157 = 12 × q + r with 0 ≤ r < 12. What is r?
quiz.explain: 12 × 13 = 156, so 157 = 12 × 13 + 1. The remainder is 1.
quiz.mistake: Gives the quotient (13) instead of the remainder

teach.ask: Gappu wants the HCF of 1071 and 462: "Listing all their factors will take forever! Is there a faster way?"
teach.praise: Euclid's algorithm: divide, take the remainder, and repeat with the smaller numbers until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the HCF. It is 21!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the remainder after the first division? When do you stop?

learn.hook: Before a robot vacuum cleans your room, someone had to think like a computer: break the job into tiny steps, repeat them and make decisions. That is algorithmic thinking!
points: Decomposition: break a big problem into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
Loops repeat a set of steps, either a fixed number of times or while a condition is true.
Conditions (if... else...) let an algorithm choose between different steps.
Flowcharts show algorithms as pictures: ovals for start and stop, rectangles for actions, diamonds for decisions (yes/no questions), and arrows for the order.
Efficiency: different algorithms can solve the same problem in very different numbers of steps. Tracing an algorithm step by step helps you find and fix bugs.

example.q: Trace this algorithm: set x = 1. While x is less than 50, replace x by 3 × x. Output x.
steps: 81 is not less than 50, so stop and output 81

learn.reallife: Indian Railways' route planning, Diwali light patterns on a timer and video games all use loops and conditions.

items.text: Breaking a big task into smaller tasks is called ___
A set of steps that repeats is called a ___
A mistake in an algorithm is often called a ___
'If marks ≥ 33, print Pass, else print Fail' is an example of a ___

quiz.q: In a flowchart, what does a diamond-shaped box show?
quiz.explain: A diamond holds a question, and the flow splits into 'yes' and 'no' paths.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the decision box with the action box

quiz.q: A total starts at 10. A loop runs 5 times, and each time it adds 4 to the total. What is the final total?
quiz.explain: 5 additions of 4 add 20, so the total becomes 10 + 20 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the starting value of 10

quiz.q: Set x = 2. While x is less than 100, replace x by x × x. What is the output?
quiz.explain: 2 → 4 → 16 → 256. 16 is still less than 100, so the loop runs once more, giving 256.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 16, forgetting to check the condition one more time

quiz.q: Which algorithm finds 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 1000 in the fewest steps?
options: Add the numbers one by one
quiz.explain: The formula needs just a multiplication and a division: 1000 × 1001 ÷ 2 = 500500, instead of 999 additions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every correct method is equally efficient

quiz.q: An algorithm says: 'If marks are 33 or more, print Pass; else print Fail.' Meena scores exactly 33. What is printed?
quiz.explain: 33 or more includes 33 itself, so the condition is true and Pass is printed.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'or more' as 'more than'

quiz.q: Harpreet's algorithm for the average of three numbers says: 'Add them, then divide by 2.' What is the correct average of 6, 9 and 12?
quiz.explain: The bug is dividing by 2. The correct average is (6 + 9 + 12) ÷ 3 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
steps: Divide by 3, the number of values
quiz.mistake: Follows the buggy step and gets 13.5

quiz.q: What is it called when you break a big problem, like planning a school trip, into smaller tasks?
quiz.explain: Decomposition means splitting a problem into parts: booking a bus, collecting money, planning food, and so on.
quiz.mistake: Confuses decomposition with repetition (looping)

quiz.q: For each of 4 rows, Kabir's algorithm says 'place 6 diyas'. How many times is a diya placed in total?
quiz.explain: The inner step runs 6 times for each of the 4 rows: 4 × 6 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Adds the loop counts instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu wants to teach a robot to water 10 plants: "Do I really have to write 'water the plant' ten times?"
teach.praise: Use a loop: repeat 'water the plant and move on' 10 times, or until no plants are left. Smart robot, smarter bird!
teach.nudge: Is there a way to tell the robot to do the same step again and again? How will it know when to stop?

learn.hook: To find all divisors of 36, do you really need to test all 36 numbers? Only up to 6!
points: divisors(n): for each j from 1 to n, check whether j divides n; if yes, add j to a list. Output the list.
The work grows with n: for n = 1000 the simple method checks 1000 numbers.
Divisors come in pairs j and n/j. One of each pair is at most √n, so you only need to check j with j × j ≤ n, and add both j and n/j.

example.q: Use the pair method to find the divisors of 60.
steps: Check j with j² ≤ 60: j = 1 to 7

learn.reallife: Packing 60 laddoos into equal boxes? Each divisor of 60 is a possible box size.

quiz.q: In the simple divisors(n) algorithm, which numbers j are tested?
quiz.explain: It checks each j in turn and keeps those that divide n.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only primes need checking

quiz.q: How many numbers does the simple algorithm test for n = 120?
quiz.mistake: Uses the pair method count

quiz.q: Using the pair idea, up to what value of j must you check for n = 120?
quiz.mistake: Checks up to n/2

quiz.q: Why can we stop checking at √n?
options: Divisors pair up as j and n/j, and one of each pair is at most √n
quiz.explain: If j > √n divides n, then n/j < √n was already found.
quiz.mistake: Thinks no divisor exceeds √n

quiz.q: How many divisors does 100 have?
quiz.mistake: Counts 10 twice

quiz.q: The simple algorithm takes 1 second for n = 1,000,000. Roughly how long for n = 10,000,000?
quiz.explain: The work grows in proportion to n.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the time grows with the number of digits

quiz.q: Which list shows all divisors of 28?
quiz.mistake: Leaves out 1 or n itself

quiz.q: For n = 49, the pair method checks j = 1 to 7. Which divisor appears without a partner?
quiz.explain: 7 × 7 = 49, so 7 pairs with itself.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every divisor has a different partner

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Do I need to test all numbers up to 100 to find the divisors of 100?"
teach.praise: Clever! Check up to √100 = 10 and use pairs to get the rest!
teach.nudge: Do divisors come alone or in pairs? Where can you stop checking?

learn.hook: Write the divisors of 24 and of 36, find what they share, pick the biggest. That's the first gcd algorithm!
points: Step 1: list divisors(m). Step 2: list divisors(n). Step 3: build the list of common divisors (numbers in both lists). Step 4: report the largest.
If the lists are sorted from smallest to largest, the gcd is the last element of the common list.
Naming intermediate results (like Dm, Dn and C) makes an algorithm clear; a list is a simple data structure for storing many values in order.

example.q: Find gcd(18, 30) with the first algorithm.

learn.reallife: Cutting two ribbons of 18 cm and 30 cm into equal pieces of the largest possible length uses the gcd: 6 cm.

games.title: First gcd algorithm
items: Build the list of common divisors

items.q: Number of common divisors of 24 and 36

quiz.q: The common divisors of 20 and 30 in sorted order are 1, 2, 5, 10. What is the gcd?
quiz.explain: The gcd is the last (largest) common divisor.
quiz.mistake: Picks the first element

quiz.q: Which list is the common divisors of 16 and 24?
quiz.mistake: Includes divisors of only one number

quiz.q: What is gcd(45, 60) by listing divisors?
quiz.explain: Common divisors: 1, 3, 5, 15.
quiz.mistake: Gives the LCM

quiz.q: In a sorted list of common divisors, why is the gcd the last element?
options: The last element is always the smaller number
It is the first number checked
The list goes from smallest to largest
quiz.explain: Sorted increasing, the largest is at the end.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the first element is the largest

quiz.q: What is a list in an algorithm?
options: A data structure that stores values in order
quiz.explain: Lists hold many values like divisors, one after another.
quiz.mistake: Confuses data with steps

quiz.q: Why does the algorithm name results like Dm, Dn and C?
options: So later steps can refer to them clearly
quiz.explain: Naming intermediate values makes each step precise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks names are decoration

quiz.q: How many common divisors do 12 and 18 have?
quiz.mistake: Counts only primes

quiz.q: Two ropes of 28 m and 42 m are cut into pieces of equal length, as long as possible, with nothing left over. How long is each piece?
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the gcd of two numbers using lists?"
teach.praise: Excellent! List both sets of divisors, find the common ones, and pick the largest!
teach.nudge: What lists do you make? Which number from the common list do you choose?

topics.title: Working with sorted lists and the LCM

learn.hook: Two sorted lists of guests: who is on the first list but not the second? Walk down both lists together!
points: To find elements of sorted list A that are not in sorted list B, walk through both with a pointer each: if the A item is smaller, it is missing from B (record it); if equal, move both; if the B item is smaller, move B's pointer.
Walking down sorted lists once is much faster than checking every element of A against every element of B.
LCM by multiples: list the multiples of the larger number (n, 2n, 3n, ...) and stop at the first one divisible by the smaller number.
Example: LCM(6, 8): multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24; 24 is divisible by 6, so LCM = 24.

example.q: A = 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 and B = 1, 5, 9, 11, 13. Which elements of A are not in B?
steps: Compare 2 with 1: move B. 2 vs 5: 2 smaller, record 2
14 vs 13: move B; B finished, record 14

learn.reallife: Buses leaving every 12 and 18 minutes meet again after LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.

items.text: A = 1, 3, 5, 7; B = 3, 7. Missing from B: 1 and ___
When the A item is smaller than the B item, it is ___ from B

quiz.q: Using multiples of the larger number, what is LCM(15, 20)?
quiz.explain: 20, 40, 60; 60 is the first divisible by 15.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the two numbers

quiz.q: How many multiples of 9 must you list to find LCM(6, 9)?
quiz.explain: 9 (not divisible by 6), 18 (divisible by 6). So 2.
quiz.mistake: Lists multiples of the smaller number

quiz.q: A = 3, 6, 9, 12 and B = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Which elements of A are not in B?
quiz.explain: 6 and 12 appear in both; 3 and 9 do not.
quiz.mistake: Lists elements of B not in A

quiz.q: Why is walking down two sorted lists together efficient?
options: It only checks the first element
Each element is looked at about once
quiz.explain: Pointers only move forward, so the work is about the total length of the lists.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every pair must be compared

quiz.q: While walking the lists, the A item is 8 and the B item is 10. What should you do?
options: Record 8 as missing from B and move A's pointer
quiz.explain: Since B is sorted and already past 8, 8 cannot be in B.
quiz.mistake: Moves the wrong pointer

quiz.q: Diyas in two rows flash every 4 seconds and every 6 seconds. After how many seconds do they flash together again?
quiz.mistake: Uses the gcd or the product

quiz.q: Which is the first multiple of 14 that is divisible by 21?
quiz.mistake: Takes the product

quiz.q: For LCM by multiples, why list multiples of the larger number?
options: The smaller number has no multiples
The LCM is always the larger number
You reach the LCM in fewer steps
quiz.explain: Bigger jumps reach the common multiple sooner.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the choice changes the answer

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the LCM of 6 and 8 using an algorithm?"
teach.praise: Great! List multiples of 8 until one is divisible by 6: 24!
teach.nudge: Which number's multiples do you list? When do you stop?

learn.hook: Why list all divisors of both numbers when you could just count down and stop at the first one that works?
points: Improvement 1: check j = 1, 2, ..., min(m, n) only, and keep just the most recent j that divides both. At the end it is the gcd. No lists needed.
Improvement 2: search downwards from min(m, n) and stop at the first j that divides both; that j is the gcd.
Each refinement must still be correct: we must explain why it always gives the gcd (for example, no common divisor can exceed the smaller number).

Efficiency: these methods need up to min(m, n) checks, which grows with the VALUE of the numbers. For a 12-digit number that could be a trillion checks, while Euclid's method grows only with the number of DIGITS.

example.q: Find gcd(84, 36) by counting down from min(84, 36).

learn.reallife: Programmers improve slow apps the same way: first make it work, then make it faster while keeping it correct.

games.title: Which version?
items: Checks every j up to min(m, n)
Last common divisor found is the gcd
First common divisor found is the gcd

games.title: Analysis
items: No common divisor of m and n can exceed min(m, n).
A divisor of n cannot be larger than n.
Counting down never needs more checks than counting up.
It stops at the gcd and never checks below it; when the gcd is 1 both need the same number.
The work of these methods depends on the number of digits only.
It depends on the value of min(m, n).
A faster algorithm need not be checked for correctness.
Euclid's method is much faster for large numbers.
Its steps grow with the number of digits.

quiz.q: In the count-up improvement, what is stored instead of full lists?
options: Only the most recent common divisor found
quiz.explain: Each time a j divides both, it replaces the stored value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks lists are still needed

quiz.q: When counting down from min(m, n), when can you stop?
options: At the first j that divides both m and n
quiz.explain: The first common divisor met while counting down is the greatest.
quiz.mistake: Keeps going to 1 unnecessarily

quiz.q: Counting down for gcd(45, 75), which j do you reach first that divides both?
quiz.explain: Start at 45: 75 ÷ 45 is not exact; ... 15 divides both.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a common divisor that is not the first from the top

quiz.q: How many checks does counting down need for gcd(40, 60)?
quiz.explain: Start at 40 and go down to 20: 40, 39, ..., 20 is 21 numbers.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to count the starting number

quiz.q: Why is it enough to check j only up to min(m, n)?
options: A common divisor must divide the smaller number, so it cannot exceed it
The gcd is always half of min(m, n)
quiz.explain: Any divisor of n is at most n.
quiz.mistake: Gives an unrelated reason

quiz.q: Counting up for gcd(m, n) where m and n are 9-digit numbers could need about how many checks?
quiz.explain: min(m, n) can be around 10⁸ or more, so that many checks.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the work depends on the number of digits

quiz.q: Which statement about efficiency is correct?
options: All gcd methods take the same time
Counting up is faster than Euclid's method
Methods whose work grows with the number of digits are much faster for big numbers
Efficiency does not matter for computers
quiz.explain: Digits grow slowly: a 12-digit number has only 12 digits but is about a trillion.
quiz.mistake: Thinks computers make efficiency irrelevant

quiz.q: A friend improves an algorithm and it runs faster but sometimes gives a wrong gcd. What is the problem?
options: The refinement was not proved correct
quiz.explain: Correctness must be justified for every change.
quiz.mistake: Values speed over correctness

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can I find the gcd faster than listing all divisors?"
teach.praise: Smart! Count down from the smaller number and stop at the first common divisor!
teach.nudge: Where should you start counting? When can you stop?

learn.hook: gcd(1000, 3) by subtracting 3 again and again takes over 300 steps. By division it takes just 2!
points: Subtraction method: gcd(m, n) = gcd(m − n, n) for m > n. Swap when m < n. Stop when one number becomes 0, since gcd(m, 0) = m.
When the numbers are very different, subtraction can take very many steps (like 1000 and 3).

Division method (Aryabhata used this repeated division in the kuttaka method of his Aryabhatiya, 499 CE, so it is called Aryabhata’s division algorithm): gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n), where m mod n is the remainder. Laid out like repeated long division: divide, then divide the divisor by the remainder, and so on, until the remainder is 0.
Why it works: if d divides m and n, it divides m − qn = remainder; and if d divides n and the remainder, it divides qn + remainder = m. So the common divisors (and the gcd) do not change.
The number of division steps grows with the number of digits, so it is very fast: it never needs more than about 5 times the number of digits of the smaller number.

example.q: Find gcd(1071, 462) by the division method.

learn.reallife: Encryption on your phone uses the division gcd algorithm many times a second because it is so fast.

quiz.q: Using subtraction, gcd(28, 12) becomes gcd(16, 12), then gcd(4, 12). What comes next?
options: Swap to gcd(12, 4), then gcd(8, 4), gcd(4, 4), gcd(0, 4) = 4
quiz.explain: Keep subtracting the smaller from the larger (swapping as needed) until one number is 0.
quiz.mistake: Stops before reaching 0

quiz.q: What is gcd(m, 0)?
quiz.explain: Every number divides 0, so the greatest common divisor of m and 0 is m.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it must be 0

quiz.q: About how many subtractions does gcd(1000, 3) need by the subtraction method?
quiz.explain: Subtracting 3 from 1000 repeatedly takes 333 steps before the numbers swap.
quiz.mistake: Thinks subtraction is as fast as division

quiz.q: What is 145 mod 12?
quiz.mistake: Gives the quotient

quiz.q: Using gcd(m, n) = gcd(n, m mod n), find gcd(156, 66).
quiz.mistake: Stops at an earlier remainder

quiz.q: How many division steps are needed for gcd(1000, 3)?
quiz.mistake: Counts subtraction steps

quiz.q: Why does d divide m mod n if d divides both m and n?
options: m mod n = m − qn, and d divides both m and qn
Because m mod n is even
quiz.explain: A number dividing two numbers divides their difference.
quiz.mistake: Cannot justify why the remainder keeps the common divisors

quiz.q: Why is the division method fast even for huge numbers?
options: Its number of steps grows with the number of digits, not the size
quiz.explain: Remainders shrink quickly, so few steps are needed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is fast only because of computers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How does the division method find the gcd so fast?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Keep dividing by the remainder; when it hits 0, the last divisor is the gcd!
teach.nudge: What replaces the larger number at each step? When do you stop?

learn.hook: The word 'algorithm' comes from a person's name. A Baghdad scholar who wrote about Indian numerals!
points: Al-Khwarizmi (9th century, Baghdad) wrote a book explaining the Indian decimal numerals and methods of calculating with them. Its Latin title began 'Algoritmi ...', and from his name came the word algorithm.
A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. So 1 is not prime (one divisor) and 4 is not prime (three divisors).
prime(n): compute divisors(n); if the list has exactly 2 elements, n is prime, otherwise it is not.
primedivisors(n): go through divisors(n) and keep only those d for which prime(d) is true. For 60: 2, 3, 5.
learn.reallife: Your phone's security uses huge primes found by prime-testing algorithms far faster than listing divisors.

quiz.q: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of:
quiz.explain: His name in Latin, Algoritmi, became 'algorithm'.
quiz.mistake: Picks another mathematician

quiz.q: Al-Khwarizmi's famous book explained:
options: the Indian decimal numerals and how to calculate with them
quiz.explain: It spread Indian place-value numerals to the Arab world and later to Europe.
quiz.mistake: Mixes him up with astronomers

quiz.q: By the definition 'exactly two divisors', why is 1 not prime?
quiz.explain: divisors(1) = 1: a list of length 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 1 has divisors 1 and 1

quiz.q: prime(n) reports TRUE when divisors(n) has how many elements?
quiz.explain: Exactly two divisors: 1 and n.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primes have one divisor

quiz.q: divisors(57) = 1, 3, 19, 57. What does prime(57) report?
quiz.explain: Four divisors, not two.
quiz.mistake: Assumes odd numbers are prime

quiz.q: What are the prime divisors of 90?
quiz.explain: divisors(90) include 9, 15 etc., but only 2, 3, 5 are prime.
quiz.mistake: Includes 1 or composite divisors

quiz.q: How many prime divisors does 210 have?
quiz.mistake: Counts all divisors

quiz.q: Which number has exactly 2 divisors?
quiz.mistake: Thinks numbers ending in 3 or 9 are prime

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can an algorithm decide if a number is prime?"
teach.praise: Perfect! List the divisors and check if there are exactly two!
teach.nudge: What list do you make first? How many elements must it have for a prime?

topics.title: Prime factorisation and gcd from factors

learn.hook: Every whole number above 1 is built from prime bricks. Record each brick and how many times it's used!
points: Prime factorisation algorithm: start with the smallest prime 2; while it divides n, divide and count; then move to the next prime. Record pairs (prime, power).
Example: 360 → divide by 2 three times (45), by 3 twice (5), by 5 once (1). Pairs: (2, 3), (3, 2), (5, 1), so 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5.
gcd from factorisations: take each prime common to both numbers with the smaller of its two powers, and multiply.
Example: 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. Common primes 2 and 3: gcd = 2² × 3¹ = 12.
learn.reallife: Cryptographers depend on the fact that factorising very large numbers is extremely slow, even though multiplying primes is easy.

quiz.q: What is the prime factorisation of 168?
quiz.mistake: Leaves a composite factor such as 14 or 21

quiz.q: In the algorithm for 360, how many times does 2 divide before moving to 3?
quiz.mistake: Stops after one division

quiz.q: Which list of (prime, power) pairs describes 600?
quiz.mistake: Misses a prime or uses composite 'primes'

quiz.q: Using factorisations, what is gcd(2⁴ × 3² × 5, 2² × 3³ × 7)?
quiz.explain: Common primes: 2 (smaller power 2) and 3 (smaller power 2): 4 × 9.
quiz.mistake: Uses the larger powers (that gives the LCM part)

quiz.explain: Common primes 2 and 3 with powers 1 and 1.
quiz.mistake: Takes all primes from both

quiz.q: If two numbers share no prime factor, their gcd is:
quiz.explain: No common primes means the only common divisor is 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is 0

quiz.q: Why does the factorisation algorithm move to the next prime only when the current one no longer divides?
options: To save time by skipping primes
Because primes must be used once
To capture the full power of each prime
quiz.explain: Dividing repeatedly counts how many times each prime appears.
quiz.mistake: Records each prime only once

quiz.q: Which number has factorisation pairs (2, 1), (3, 1), (11, 1)?
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one of the primes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I get the gcd from prime factorisations?"
teach.praise: Superb! Take the common primes with their smaller powers and multiply!
teach.nudge: Which primes do you use? Which power of each do you take?
